title: Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams
mutable_substrate: A bounded LLM-agent harness comprising prompts, skills, tools, memory, supporting infrastructure, and regime-specific git branches; model weights remain fixed.
optimization_operator: A stateful four-phase multi-agent evolver (Analyst, three parallel Researchers, Builder, Verifier) analyzes temporally revealed trajectories, researches missing capabilities, edits harness files, tests changes, and creates or retires specialized branches. A Sonnet router selects a branch per task.
feedback_selection: Chronological execution feedback enters through a temporal-reveal gate: trajectories are available immediately, while labels appear only after resolution. An Expected-Gain-from-Learning trigger (threshold 0.05, window 3) gates cycles. Verification is a pre-release PASS/FAIL gate; solve-time selection uses task context and branch README signals at a 0.7 confidence threshold. Human hooks can add credentials or source guidance when history lacks signal.
archive_memory: A persistent evolver workspace stores task_board.md, research_log.jsonl, architecture notes, verifier reports, tests, observations, and strategy_tree.md. Solver harnesses are isolated and versioned as a git tree with main and regime-specific branches.
validation_strategy: Full chronological runs on three streams; five auto-harness baselines, five no-evolution solver models, and OctoTools; no-memory and no-feedback ablations; benchmark bottleneck diagnostics; all-branch replay with Oracle/Adapt/Naive/Worst controls and corrected paired tests; per-category analyses; a logged 100-task HITL study; temperature-zero point estimates.
adaptation_mode: Continual offline-between-batch harness evolution plus online solve-time routing among prebuilt branches. Human task-board or research-phase interventions occur only at structurally defined hooks.
benchmarks: PolyBench: 5,075 prediction-market tasks, 2026-02-06 to 2026-02-22, Accuracy and coverage-scaled confidence-weighted Return
CTF-Dojo: 261 chronological security challenges from 2011 to 2024, Pass@1
FutureX: 503 English/Chinese event-forecasting tasks from 2026-01 to 2026-04, Pass@1
principal_results: Full System reaches 97.9% PolyBench coverage, 80.9% Accuracy, and +330% Return; Adaptive has the best Return at +352%, and Multi-agent scores 79.8% Accuracy and +351% Return.
Full System reaches 50.2% CTF-Dojo Pass@1 versus 45.2% A-Evolve and 37.2% no-evolution Sonnet.
Multi-agent leads FutureX at 49.5% Pass@1; Full System scores 47.3%, A-Evolve 47.5%, and Adaptive 44.1%, showing routing is not universally additive.
On curated ablations, stateful multi-agent evolution improves single-agent results from 20.3 to 44.3 CWR on PolyBench, 38% to 43% on CTF-Dojo, and 38% to 44% on FutureX.

Oracle-minus-Naive branch headroom is +37.5 points on CTF-Dojo (Holm-adjusted p=4.8e-4) and +8.8 CWR points on PolyBench (p=1.8e-5); Adapt recovers +17.5 and +2.7 respectively but loses 5.2 points to Naive on FutureX.
Targeted HITL steering yields slice lifts of 0, +5, +20, +15, and 0 points across five FutureX regimes.
limitations: The formal evolution and adaptation losses depend on unavailable oracle quantities and are diagnosed only through proxies.
The three finite retrospective streams do not demonstrate indefinite deployment or monotonic improvement; Multi-agent peaks at cycle 22/51 on PolyBench and 10/26 on FutureX.
The appendix prose says CTF-Dojo utility accumulates across all 14 cycles, but its table reports peak cycle 1.
Routing analysis seeds category branches and uses smaller exhaustive replay subsets; the live router trails main on FutureX and never selects its allowed main fallback in the analyzed subsets.
Results use closed hosted models at temperature zero without repeated-run uncertainty estimates.
Evolver-side tokens and orchestration overhead were not persisted, so total cost is unknown.
FutureX Chinese entertainment remains at 0% for every reported system, and large CTF payloads remain a major failure mode.
HITL evidence comes from author interventions using a pre-authored cheat sheet rather than independent operators.
safety_controls: Temporal-reveal gating prevents outcome labels from entering evolution before resolution.
FutureX uses cutoff-aware Wikipedia/search/structured-data retrieval and an LLM filter that redacts post-cutoff evolved-tool output.
CTF-Dojo runs in isolated per-task Docker containers with constrained networking and hash-based flag verification.
Builder changes require verifier PASS before release and can be retried at most three times.
Git branches isolate regime-specific artifacts; the Analyst audits toxic shortcuts and can deprecate or relocate them.
Human credentials are redacted, and humans may guide sources or access but may not provide answers or choose solver branches.

explicit_predecessors.name: A-Evolve
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Directly extends and critiques its linear-chain, execution-feedback harness evolution by adding persistent multi-agent roles and branch isolation.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related Work explicitly describes A-Evolve as a linear-chain evolver that mutates prompts, skills, memory, and tools; Figure 1 uses an A-Evolve stream to demonstrate dense-harness regression.

explicit_predecessors.name: GEPA
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Methodological predecessor and main auto-harness baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related Work explicitly identifies GEPA's reflective Pareto prompt evolution from textual feedback, and Table 2 compares it on all three streams.

explicit_predecessors.name: Meta-Harness
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Filesystem-based harness-evolution predecessor and main baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related Work explicitly names its growing filesystem archive and Claude Code proposer; the experiments compare it directly.

explicit_predecessors.name: Continual Harness
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Online continual-adaptation predecessor whose continuous action/refinement cycle addresses the same deployment regime with a different update structure.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related Work explicitly states that Continual Harness adapts online within one continuous deployment run, and it is evaluated as a baseline.

explicit_predecessors.name: SkillOS
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Skill-selection predecessor contrasted with whole-harness branch routing.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related Work explicitly describes SkillOS as an RL-trained curator that selects and refines reusable skills; Table 2 includes it as an auto-harness baseline.

open_questions: How can evolution and adaptation loss be estimated without an unattainable full-history oracle or exhaustive branch replay?
Can a release criterion guarantee non-degradation or bounded regret when later evolution cycles overfit?
How should branch creation, merging, retirement, and main fallback be jointly optimized under compute and latency budgets?
Can router feedback improve selection without leaking outcomes or collapsing all specialization into the main branch?
Will the design sustain performance on genuinely indefinite, live streams with delayed feedback and unanticipated regimes?
What is the full end-to-end cost once evolver tokens, orchestration, verification retries, and human wait time are counted?
How should credentials, network-capable evolved tools, and human-provided endpoints be sandboxed and audited against prompt injection and secret exfiltration?
